entry.title: Cult Hit ‘Hundreds of Beavers’ Returns to Theaters for Big Christmas Expansion
entry.summary: Cult hit 'Hundreds of Beavers' is returning to theaters this Christmas across 85 cities and 130 screenings.
entry.content:
It’s been four years since the cult hit “Hundreds of Beavers” first debuted and still two years since it started really gaining traction with wider audiences in 2024. But if it feels like the black and white, silent, slapstick indie comedy still hasn’t left the cultural conversation, that’s because in all that time it has continued to quietly play in theaters and attract audiences both loyal and new alike.

Technically, “Hundreds of Beavers” has never left theaters. It continues to play individual screenings in a city or two every weekend. Now, though, “Hundreds of Beavers” is set to return to theaters for what is its biggest theatrical expansions to date. The film will kick off its third annual Northwoods Christmas, which will feature 130 screenings across 85 cities, with more to likely be added in the coming weeks. It came about after another fan campaign pushed for the film to come to some markets it hadn’t previously thought about or targeted such as Indianapolis and Charlottesville, and it will now play in everything from concert venues to microcinemas.

Related Stories
Cinematographer Caleb Deschanel on Finding the Right Techniques For ‘The Right Stuff’
Where Are Rick Dalton and Sharon Tate in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?

The re-releases have become a holiday tradition for “Hundreds of Beavers,” which for all its wintery setting and its main character dressed like Santa, is being positioned as a new Christmas movie. The first time “Hundreds of Beavers” was re-released at Christmas 2024, which was shortly after the Blu-ray for the film became available, it brought in $118K at the box office in a month, and the producers continued the tradition in 2025.

“There’s room for a Christmas tradition with the energy of a ‘Rocky Horror’ screening,” said producer Kurt Ravenwood. “You can watch ‘It’s a Wonderful Life’ and ‘White Christmas’ all you want, but for getting together with friends and family to laugh about the miserable winter ahead, ‘Hundreds of Beavers’ has them all beat.”

Each of the screenings will be preceded by a short film featuring “Bing Crosbeaver,” which they did last year, but this will be a new short with a new twist in which another character named “Conspirabeaver” will be joined by a “sinister foe,” per the release. Some of the in-person beavers in costume will be present at the screenings, and fans will also get a promotional poster for the movie. The “Beavers” team recently released a few parody posters ripping off the recent releases of “You Can See Everything,” “Digger,” and “The Devils.”

To date, “Hundreds of Beavers” has made $940,092 at the domestic box office, including another $618,014 internationally to bring its worldwide total to above $1.5 million. It’s done all this via first producing the film for just $150,000 and spending little more than $70,000 on ads, publicity, and its many roadshow screenings. It’s also been released entirely independently, starting with a run in the Midwest where the film is set before it started expanding to the coasts.

Incredibly, more than 70 percent of the film’s U.S. box office has come after “Hundreds of Beavers” began streaming way back on April 15, 2024, and it has even sold more than 20,000 Blu-Rays worldwide. It’s a rare, truly indie success story even in a day and age when many movies have pursued self-distribution strategies.

For those who haven’t had the pleasure of seeing “Hundreds of Beavers” in theaters yet, the film is about a drunken applejack salesman who loses everything and has to survive the winter by becoming North America’s greatest fur trapper. It sees the trapper wrestling and fighting with dozens of beavers and other forest animals all wearing mascot suits, with the stark black and white cinematography and creative physical stunts embracing a zany video game logic and absurd silent comedy slapstick gags.

The film is directed by Mike Cheslik and was written by Cheslik and star Ryland Tews, with the film also starring Olivia Graves, Wes Tank, Doug Mancheski, and Luis Rico.

entry.title: Cinematographer Caleb Deschanel on Finding the Right Techniques For ‘The Right Stuff’
entry.summary: The director of photography discusses working with Philip Kaufman, Ed Harris, and more on the classic film about the space race, new to Criterion.
entry.content:
“The Right Stuff” was released 43 years ago, but its spectacular aerial and outer space sequences have lost none of their power. Director Philip Kaufman’s adaptation of Tom Wolfe’s book, which traced the history of the test pilots who became the first astronauts, features immersive set pieces that are still as convincing as ever, in spite of decades of technological advancements since it was made. To revisit it via Criterion‘s new 4K UHD physical media release is to experience one of the most groundbreaking and enduring films of all time.

The new Criterion transfer was supervised by cinematographer Caleb Deschanel, who was still relatively early in his career when Kaufman tapped him to shoot “The Right Stuff.” Deschanel didn’t have many feature credits, but the ones he did have were impressive: his early work included the stunning imagery of “The Black Stallion” and two Hal Ashby movies, “Being There” and the Rolling Stones concert film “Let’s Spend the Night Together.” He would earn the first of his six Academy Award nominations for “The Right Stuff.”

Related Stories
Where Are Rick Dalton and Sharon Tate in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?
‘Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo’ Will Come to the U.S. Next March

Deschanel had met Kaufman years earlier when Deschanel was a film student at USC, and Kaufman was a young director working on the Western “The Great Northfield Minnesota Raid.” “A couple friends and I put on these rock shows at Shrine Auditorium, and he came to a couple of those,” Deschanel told IndieWire. Deschanel visited the set of “Minnesota” and stayed in touch with Kaufman, who called him around 10 years later with the offer to shoot “The Right Stuff.”

“It was a dream come true,” Deschanel said, noting that he had always been an aviation buff who loved going to air shows with his father. He also remembered that Kaufman wasn’t the only person on “The Right Stuff” who he had met years earlier. “Years before we had moved into our first house and needed some painting done, and we had a friend who was teaching in the Cal Arts theater department. He said, ‘I have this actor who’s really great who paints houses in the summer.'”

Deschanel hired the young actor and got to know him a little bit, and five years later was having lunch with his wife Mary Jo and Kaufman when Kaufman showed them a picture of the actor he had chosen to play John Glenn. “I said, ‘We know him. That’s Ed Harris. He painted our house,'” Deschanel said. “Then, coincidentally, the woman who was supposed to play Annie Glenn dropped out of and Phil cast my wife, so they ended up playing husband and wife in the movie.”

One of the great technical challenges of “The Right Stuff” was integrating archival footage of the space race with the new material being shot — one of the reasons the movie was shot in a 1.85:1 aspect ratio instead of a wider Panavision format as one might have expected for such an epic film. “We were using actual footage of NASA’s rocket launches and things like that, and they were filming in the old-fashioned 4:3 format using the full frame of a 35mm camera,” Deschanel said. “Converting that to widescreen was really impossible.”

Working in close collaboration with visual effects supervisor Gary Gutierrez (who provides a fascinating look at the film’s miniature and rear-projection work on the Criterion disc), Deschanel solved the numerous logistical problems that came with trying to make it look as though the actors were hurtling through the air at the speed of sound and beyond. Even when Gutierrez thought he had solutions that would work, they often had to be tweaked to accommodate Kaufman’s desire to make everything feel as realistic and immersive as possible.

Early attempts to use a motion-control system for the effects, for example, were discarded because the camera movement was too smooth for Kaufman’s purposes. “Phil wanted it to have some energy to it,” Deschanel said. “That changed the whole methodology.” Whenever rockets were taking off or various crafts were flying, Deschanel made sure to add some shake to the camera. “I actually gave my camera operator, Craig Denault, a black eye at one point because I was hitting the camera so hard.”

In addition to the expected challenges, there were plenty of unexpected ones as well — like the fact that Sam Shepard, who played ace pilot Chuck Yeager, wouldn’t fly. “The only time he ever went up in an airplane was when Yeager took him for a flight,” Deschanel said. “Other than that, whenever we had a mockup of an X-1 or the F-104 or anything like that, he’d make me get in and show him how it was going to twist and turn before he would get into it.” For Yeager’s scenes and many of the others, rear projection was used — meaning Deschanel had to photograph what was seen outside the pilots’ and astronauts’ windows long before the actors’ material was actually shot.

“There was a lot of complexity to all those things,” Deschanel said. “But it gave it a real energy and sense of being there. And that’s what you try to discover as you’re filming any film: what is that visual metaphor that really makes you believe you’re having the same experience the characters are having?” Creating that sense of authenticity required some unorthodox approaches, as when Deschanel had a Learjet pilot take the nose cone off of his plane and replace it with a clear dome.

“We put a camera in there with a 15mm lens, and then we were able to go up above 50,000 feet,” Deschanel said. “At that level, it’s so dark, it’s almost like you’re in outer space. Anything you could think of to find the reality of the movie, we employed.” Deschanel’s perfectionism became the stuff of legend over the years, with some people who worked on “The Right Stuff” claiming he insisted on shooting only at sunrise or sunset to get the most beautiful possible images — a myth Deschanel is quick to dispel.

“The fact is we shot all day long and had really long days,” Deschanel said. “There was one point where, just to finish up at Edwards Air Force Base, I was on for 24 hours and changed the crew in the middle. So I had a whole new crew for the second half of that long day.” That said, Deschanel acknowledges that the film’s justly famous exteriors were important to him, in part for what they represented.

“The iconic moment is when Yeager is on horseback, and he rides up and sees the X-1,” Deschanel said. “It’s like ‘The Professionals’ or ‘The Wild Bunch,’ these movies about the end of the West as new technology takes over. To me, there’s this wonderful representation of the end of an era when Yeager comes across this fighter jet. Then, of course, he flies it and breaks the sound barrier. So it’s this wonderful juxtaposition of important moments in human history, where one person does something that further advances flight to the point that makes it possible for the next generation to go into outer space. I always miss that I never got to make a Western, but in a way, ‘The Right Stuff’ is a Western.”

“The Right Stuff” special edition 4K UHD release is now available from Criterion.

entry.title: Where Are Rick Dalton and Sharon Tate in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’?
entry.summary: Only 'Once Upon a Time in Hollywood' lead is back for 'Cliff Booth,' but that doesn't mean Rick Dalton and Sharon Tate don't pop up in other ways.
entry.content:
[Editor’s note: This article contains small spoilers for “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.”]

It should come as little surprise that David Fincher’s “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” focuses on, well, Cliff Booth. The Quentin Tarantino-penned sequel to the filmmaker’s own 2019 Oscar-winning hit “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” has always been billed as a spinoff following the continuing adventures of his fictitious (yet still iconic) stuntman Cliff Booth (Brad Pitt). But Tarantino has always loved building out his own shared and connected universe(s), and fans sure love exploring its outer limits.

“Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” and, by extension, “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” occupy a unique place in Tarantino’s cinematic world, as they’re both part of his so-called “Realer Than Real World Universe” and his “Movie Movie Universe.” Tarantino didn’t just keep crafting his movies-within-movies world with the hit film — he also introduced real-world (realer than real world?) elements and people (the Mansion Family, of course, and all that entails).

Related Stories
‘Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo’ Will Come to the U.S. Next March
‘The Trip’ Returns for Fifth Installment, Next Sending Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon to Frigid Arctic Circle

That bent continues in “Cliff Booth,” which is rife with both out-there elements and very real references (time for that “Hee Haw” resurgence, we guess). But the film also has to follow its own series logic, which means, yes, it’s the Cliff Booth show, but hey, where are our “Hollywood” co-stars Rick Dalton (Leonardo DiCaprio) and Sharon Tate (Margot Robbie)?

[Once again: This article contains small spoilers for “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.”]

Rick Dalton

When we first meet Cliff and Rick, the duo are long-time colleagues and best pals. As his stunt double, Cliff is tasked with doing some serious heavy lifting for Hollywood star Rick, which inevitably (?) leads them to off four members of the Mansion Family. The raucous and wild violence the duo inflicts on the foursome isn’t just a fun bonding exercise for the pair. It also ensures that the nefarious group can’t go next door to enact the infamous (and very real) Tate murders. Win-win!

The film ends with an invitation for Rick to slide on over to the Tate house for a thank-you drink, presumably putting him in the path of Roman Polanski, Sharon, and all the star power they carry. “Cliff Booth” is set eight years after those events, and while Rick may have enjoyed a career upswing in the interim, his current professional endeavors have taken him far from Hollywood.

While we never see Rick in the film (despite ongoing rumors that DiCaprio might appear for a quick cameo), Cliff mentions him frequently and fondly, including telling potential paramour Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki) that their professional entanglements ended when Rick got, ahem, “too fat” for Cliff to believably double him and then moved to Australia to star in the TV series “Dingo Dan.” Further details on the show are slim, but we do know it’s a Western TV show that’s proven quite popular and durable (Aussie Karen seems to like it), and Cliff makes it sound like Rick is enjoying himself. Not too bad.

Sharon Tate

By blending his two movie universes with “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” Tarantino got to both delight in late-’60s Hollywood magic and “save” Sharon Tate, her unborn son, Abigail Folger, Wojciech Frykowski, Steven Parent, and Jay Sebring. That sort of revisionist history was the film’s buzziest twist and, as I argued at the time, the most emotional choice Tarantino has ever made in his filmography.

And while we don’t get treated to much more Sharon in “Cliff Booth,” we are granted some, in the form of a Red Apple Cigarettes commercial led by a beaming Margot Robbie, returning to her original role as the doomed actress. (The fake cigarettes are another Tarantino-verse staple, and Rick even appears in his own commercial for them during the end credits of “Hollywood.”)

In the short cameo, Sharon looks healthy and happy, and she’s clearly still enough of a star to warrant her own advertising campaign, built on her smile and her zippy shimmy. As Cliff watches the commercial at the Marina del Rey condo he shares with his dad (Peter Weller), he takes the time to stop, observe, and notably smile at the star. It’s a small grace note, and a very effective one.

One other star of “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” is missing from “Cliff Booth,” though. Just where the heck is Brandy?

Netflix will release “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” in IMAX theaters on Wednesday, November 25. It will be available to stream on Netflix starting Wednesday, December 23.

entry.title: ‘Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo’ Will Come to the U.S. Next March
entry.summary: Neon will release 'Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo' in the U.S. on March 5, 2027.
entry.content:
“Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo,” a Japan-set take on police decadence, will open in North America on March 5, 2027. Neon, the Oscar-winning studio behind “Anora” and “Parasite,” is distributing the film.

Directed by Takashi Miike, the Japanese auteur behind “Audition” and “13 Assassins,” “”Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo” stars Shun Oguri (“Godzilla v. Kong”), Lily James (“Pam and Tommy”), and WWE star Liv Morgan. It follows a veteran police detective Yabuki (Oguri), who is struggling with drug addiction, gambling debts, and guilt over past misdeeds, as he chases a shadowy killer tied to organized crime through Tokyo. His case ends up intersecting with that of an American FBI agent (James), who’s hunting a missing tourist (Morgan).

Related Stories
‘The Trip’ Returns for Fifth Installment, Next Sending Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon to Frigid Arctic Circle
‘The Holy Boy’ Review: A Teenage Boy Heals People with His Touch in an Eerie Italian Horror Movie About the Price of Avoiding Your Pain

The film had its world premiere at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival, where it earned mixed notices, with some reviewers faulting it as overstuffed. Neon is in the midst of a busy fall, with the indie studio releasing awards contenders such as “All of a Sudden,” “Fjord,” “Paper Tiger,” and “Artificial,” so it makes sense that it would opt to have “Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo” come out in the spring.

“Bad Lieutenant” first entered the cinematic vernacular with Abel Ferrara’s 1992 crime thriller that was so boundary-pushing (a nun is raped) it received an NC-17 rating. It also offered up Harvey Keitel at his most unhinged and committed, playing a cop who broke really, really bad. Then Werner Herzog transported the depravity to the Big Easy with 2009’s “Bad Lieutenant: Port of Call New Orleans,” featuring Nicolas Cage at his most gonzo. Thus, an unlikely franchise was born.

The latest “Bad Lieutenant” is a U.S.-Japan co-production, produced by the late Jeremy Thomas for Recorded Picture Company, Sam Pressman for Pressman Film, Naoaki Kitajima for Nippon TV, and Misako Saka for OLM.

entry.title: ‘The Trip’ Returns for Fifth Installment, Next Sending Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon to Frigid Arctic Circle
entry.summary: 'The Trip to the Northern Lights,' the fifth film in 'The Trip' comedy franchise, has been acquired by IFC and will hit theaters April 9, 2027.
entry.content:
What does “Michael Caine” sound like in the freezing cold? We’re about to find out with the just-announced release of “The Trip to the Northern Lights,” which is the reunion of Steve Coogan, Rob Brydon, and director Michael Winterbottom for what is the fifth installment of “The Trip” franchise of miniseries/movies.

Independent Film Company and Sapan Studio picked up the U.S. rights to the fifth “Trip” film (IFC has released all four of the other films into theaters in the U.S.) and will release it theatrically on April 9, 2027. It will have been nearly seven years since the release of the last feature, and it sees Brydon now at 60 and Coogan at 59, so we’re guessing their ages may have made their wit and appetites even more ornery since.

Related Stories
‘The Holy Boy’ Review: A Teenage Boy Heals People with His Touch in an Eerie Italian Horror Movie About the Price of Avoiding Your Pain
‘The Mosquito Bowl’ Review: ‘Friday Night Lights’ Meets ‘Five Came Back’ in Peter Berg’s Formulaic Netflix Movie About a World War II Football Game

“The Trip” movies are known for their food and travel porn as much as they are for their litany of impressions between Coogan and Brydon playing versions of themselves, but this one turns that concept on its head slightly by sending Coogan and Brydon up north, this time throughout Scandinavia, including Sweden and some islands in Norway, all in search of some other fine food and wry conversation.

The first look at the movie above sees the duo in ridiculously huge parkas in the snow as guided by some sled huskies. Try doing your best Bane impression at 10 below zero.

“We are very happy to be back on the road with IFC. They have been brilliant partners ever since the first ‘Trip’ all those years ago. ‘The Trip to the Northern Lights‘ takes Steve and Rob from Malmo in southern Sweden through Norway’s spectacular fjords to the Lofoten Islands in Norway’s Arctic circle,” Winterbottom said. “I hope the audience enjoys the journey as much as we did.”

“The Trip” franchise began all the way back in 2011, and since then the films have spanned trips in England, Italy, Spain, and Greece. As has been the case with all of the installments, they’ve been miniseries airing on TV in England but then edited into films for the U.S. release. The first movie made $3.9 million worldwide across several re-releases, “The Trip to Italy” in 2014 made $6.1 million, 2017’s “The Trip to Spain” made $1.9 million, and “The Trip to Greece” in the COVID-addled summer 2020 still managed to make $259K worldwide.

All four of the “Trip” movies are currently available for streaming on Sun Now, which is the streamer owned by Independent Film Company parent AMC Global Media.

“The Independent Film Company is thrilled to continue our longstanding relationship with this world-class group of filmmakers on the latest installment of this beloved franchise. Few comedic partnerships have the enduring appeal of Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon, and under Michael Winterbottom’s inspired direction, each new trip remains the comedic gift that keeps on giving. This time around, we can’t wait for audiences to join us on the road to the Northern Lights,” said Ayo Kepher-Maat, Independent Film Company’s Vice President of Acquisitions and Production.

“Michael Winterbottom, Steve Coogan, and Rob Brydon have created a franchise filled with taste, wit and belly laughs. Independent Film Company has brought each one to audiences with characteristic care and capability. ‘The Trip to the Northern Lights’ advances the history with the delight of something completely fresh and tasty,” said Josh Sapan of Sapan Studio.

The film is produced by Melissa Parmenter and Josh Hyams for Revolution Films. The deal was negotiated by Ayo Kepher-Maat on behalf of Independent Film Company and Tristan Whalley MD of Goalpost Films on behalf of the filmmakers.

Executive producers are Winterbottom, Coogan, Brydon, Alex Moody, Josh Sapan, Tristan Whalley, Paul Wiegard. “The Trip to the Northern Lights” is a Revolution Films, Baby Cow, and Small Man Production in association with Sky Studios.

Deadline first reported the news of the acquisition.

entry.title: ‘The Holy Boy’ Review: A Teenage Boy Heals People with His Touch in an Eerie Italian Horror Movie About the Price of Avoiding Your Pain
entry.summary: Rising horror director Paolo Strippoli makes a name for himself with a confident genre allegory about the dangers of waiting for a miracle.
entry.content:
In March 2009, a train crash kills 46 people near a picturesque village nestled deep within the Italian Alps. In the present day, an alcoholic gym teacher named Sergio (Michele Riondino) — nursing some recent grief of his own — is relocated to Remis, only to find that the surviving townspeople have never been happier, despite the shared tragedy that would seem to overshadow their lives.

It’s uncanny. It’s disturbing. It’s what Sergio wants for himself more than anything in the world. And he’s told that all he has to do to make the pain go away is to hug “The Holy Boy” mentioned in the English title of Paolo Strippoli’s third feature, a slick and effectively spine-tickling horror movie about the harm sown into people convinced they can avoid their own hurt. (It’s also one hell of a calling card for the young Italian director, whose recent festival hit “The Spiral” will receive an Oscar-qualifying release later this year, and an English-language remake sometime after that).

Related Stories
‘The Mosquito Bowl’ Review: ‘Friday Night Lights’ Meets ‘Five Came Back’ in Peter Berg’s Formulaic Netflix Movie About a World War II Football Game
Lauren Ambrose on Playing the Mother of a Missing Teen in ‘The Unbelievers’ and Why ‘Six Feet Under’ Is a Hit with Gen Z

For a time, Sergio becomes one of those people. When he first arrives in Remis, sobbing in his car as it chugs up the curvy mountain roads, it feels like a cruel joke that the surly ex-Judo champion has been relocated to a place known as “The Valley of Smiles.” He’s a belligerent asshole to the kids in his P.E. class, acts violently toward the beautiful waitress (Romana Maggiora Vergano as Michela) at the local bar, and generally brings a “Bad Santa” energy to a town with more of a “Pleasantville” vibe.

But from the start, it’s clear Remis hides a secret darkness — a darkness so deep that none of the residents can see clearly that they live in a horror film. It isn’t normal for a weasel-eyed man to stand in the bushes and glare at the village high school all day. It isn’t normal for everyone to meet in a barn on the outskirts of town in the middle of the night and participate in a vaguely Catholic ritual that sees them all line up for a chance to lay their hands on a sullen 15-year-old kid (Giulio Feltri as Matteo). It isn’t normal for them to feel like they might go insane, or worse, if they go too long without his touch. Give people a panacea for their pain, and they’ll do anything to keep it, logic be damned.

Of course, logic is hardly the only thing that’s damned in “The Holy Boy,” whose concussive soundtrack, broadly demonic symbology (e.g., dropped coins transforming into bloody egg yolks), and genre-inflected visual motifs (lots of upside-down camerawork and clever uses of soft focus) help consecrate this high-altitude “Twilight Zone” story’s rather literal approach to elevated horror. But Strippoli’s script, co-written by Jacopo Del Giudice and Milo Tissone, isn’t content to settle for mere social allegory, even if the movie tacks harder in that direction with every new detail we learn about Matteo’s effect on the people who touch him. On the contrary, the film’s excellent second act — during which Sergio is fully seduced by the town’s healing power and even settles into a sexual relationship with Michaela — leverages its premise in service of a tenderly ominous character study.

Closeted, sanctified, and at the mercy of a purpose that he never chose for himself, Matteo struggles to see his gift as a miracle; if anything, he worries that it’s more like a curse in disguise. It was, perhaps, easier for him to live with (and be used for) when he was a child, but the self-determination of teenage desire has complicated his relationship to the power he embodies. It’s not just that nobody understands Matteo, or cares to — he also struggles to understand himself. If the local bully is so mean to him at school every day, why does Matteo touch himself when he thinks about him at night? The answer may be obvious, but it doesn’t bring peace to the boy’s tormented heart, which pumps with a pain no one else in town allows themselves to feel. Not even Sergio, whose curiosity toward Matteo proves humanizing — and the basis for a real friendship — even as he grows addicted to the child’s power himself.

It’s here, between the smiling eeriness of its first act and the somewhat “Akira”-coded psychic collapse of its third, that “The Holy Boy” settles into its skin-crawling purpose. The film is at its most confident and secure as a “Thelma”-like coming-of-age story that weaponizes teenage growing pains against the world at large, as Matteo’s limitless potential is poisoned by the unmet needs of the wanting and selfish people around him. In his own way, and despite his best efforts, Sergio is such a person himself, even if he’s still close enough to his own heartache to see Matteo more clearly than most.

But Strippoli is only interested in Sergio as a way to push back against Matteo’s power (and therefore escalate things to the wild places they go before arriving at the film’s satisfying final beat). A richer pas de deux that probes deeper into the grown man’s loss — and his rather complicated history of fathering teenage boys — is gradually sacrificed at the altar of social commentary.

Religion and fascism are Strippoli’s most obvious targets, but “The Holy Boy” is wary of anything that people rely on to absolve them of their pain, and of how the things we turn to for comfort are liable to control us the moment we convince ourselves to believe in miracles. Touched by evil from the moment it starts, Strippoli’s film never invites the kind of faith from its audience that it abuses from its characters en masse, but I didn’t have any trouble believing the moral of its twisted sermon: Keep your pain alive, as it might be the only thing protecting you from something so much worse.

Grade: B

“The Holy Boy” will be available to stream on Shudder starting Friday, November 27.

entry.title: Lauren Ambrose on Playing the Mother of a Missing Teen in ‘The Unbelievers’ and Why ‘Six Feet Under’ Is a Hit with Gen Z
entry.summary: Lauren Ambrose talks about her Off-Broadway play 'The Unbelievers' and discusses 'Six Feet Under's' popularity with Gen Z.
entry.content:
Lauren Ambrose sounds almost embarrassed to admit that she was puzzled the first time she read the script for Nick Payne’s “The Unbelievers.” “I was like, ‘Oh my God, what is this? I don’t understand this at all,'” Ambrose told IndieWire, scrunching up her face in a mask of bewilderment. “What’s he getting at?”

The drama, which is wrapping up its limited run at the Manhattan Theatre Club this month, is elliptical, moving backward and forward in time as it follows Miriam’s search for her missing son, Oscar. That description sounds like a thousand thrillers, but “The Unbelievers” resists easy classification — it’s a narratively daring story, overflowing with ideas about grief and faith and family.

Related Stories
‘Paper Tiger’: James Gray Convinced Adam Driver He Was Playing the Hero, Then Crafted His Mythic End
‘All of a Sudden’ Review: Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s Long and Thoughtful Plea for a More Hopeful Future

It was only after doing a workshop for the play that Ambrose discovered that what she initially found so alienating about “The Unbelievers” was actually its greatest strength. “There’s a lot to talk about, and a lot to parse, and a lot to think about, and it’s highly interpretable and analyzable, and I think that’s actually a marker of good art is that it can be interpreted in many ways,” Ambrose said over Zoom, hours before she was set to take the stage again.

The role of Miriam is almost Everest-like in its difficulty. As the years pass without any sign of Oscar — not knowing if he’s been kidnapped or murdered or ran away — Miriam becomes more obsessed, more unmoored by the lack of resolution. That strains her relationship with her two daughters and Oliver’s father, who are processing their grief in different ways and worry that Miriam is growing fanatical in her insistence that he may still be out there.

“It’s fun in a perverse way to go on this crazy journey every night,” Ambrose said. “There are all these wild turns. It’s tiring vocally. My body hurts, my neck is messed up. But it’s amazing to get to play a part like this. You just have to throw yourself off a cliff.”

Ambrose made a name for herself in films like “Can’t Hardly Wait” and on “Six Feet Under,” where she played Claire Fisher, a rebellious dreamer growing up in her family-run funeral home. The show debuted in 2001 on HBO, where it aired alongside “The Sopranos” and “Sex and the City” at the peak of the cable channel’s cultural supremacy. Decades later, “Six Feet Under” has been rediscovered on streaming by Gen Z, giving it an unexpected surge in popularity.

“It was a golden age,” Ambrose said. “We were making these hour-long films each week. And HBO was so open and supportive of creative people. The attitude was, if you want to try something, try it. There weren’t algorithms determining everything. That freedom is palpable with the series, so I think that’s why it’s resonating and why it’s being embraced by this new generation.”

Ambrose remains in demand on the big and small screen, recently appearing on another water-cooler hit, Showtime’s “Yellowjackets.” But she’s made a point of returning to the stage throughout her career, appearing on Broadway in “Exit the King” and “Awake and Sing!,” as well as earning a Tony Award nomination playing Eliza Doolittle in a revival of “My Fair Lady.”

“I love the stage — I love it so much,” Ambrose said. “I love a rehearsal room. It’s my favorite place in the world. It’s where you’re figuring it out and making connections. But a play is always a living thing. We’ve opened ‘The Unbelievers,’ but I haven’t stopped my work of trying to scavenge around and figure out this mysterious character.”

entry.title: ‘Paper Tiger’: James Gray Convinced Adam Driver He Was Playing the Hero, Then Crafted His Mythic End
entry.summary: Writer/director James Gray breaks down the ending of 'Paper Tiger' and the fate of Adam Driver's unlikely hero.
entry.content:
Editor’s Note: The following story contains spoilers for “Paper Tiger.”

One night, after his second child was born, James Gray found himself up late watching C-SPAN coverage of the Global Economic Forum in Davos, and saw something he held onto for years.

“This corporate CEO said, ‘95% of people don’t know there’s a game, and they lose,'” said Gray on IndieWire’s Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast. “Of the remaining 5%, 4% know there’s a game and don’t know how to play it, and 1% knows there’s a game and wins. And he said it with evident pride. I thought it revolting.”

The CEO’s words hit home for Gray, showing a “cruel economic system that people can’t control,” where luck, timing, and “having skills that are popular at the right time” decide who wins.

Related Stories
‘All of a Sudden’ Review: Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s Long and Thoughtful Plea for a More Hopeful Future
‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ Made Nearly $4 Billion Doing What Movies Can’t

“I would love a system where everyone got rewarded, not one that picks winners and losers,” said Gray. “The idea of losers breaks my heart. The film was about my heartbreak over the world’s losers.”

The script for “Paper Tiger” centers on three lead characters, each representing a different side of Gray’s cautionary tale about the dangers of chasing the American Dream. Of his three main characters, Gary (Adam Driver) is best positioned to be one of the “winners.”

“[Gary] is the one person who knows the game, knows how to play it, and just [can’t] live with himself if he makes certain choices that might allow him to, quote-unquote, ‘win,’” said Gray of Driver’s character. “We don’t see that much in movies. We see people who are ‘bad guys’ who make the wrong choice, or ‘good guys’ who make the right choice and then wind up winning for it.”

Gary, the ex-cop turned savvy businessman, presents himself as comfortable crossing that ethical line, but as the story slowly reveals, a strong moral code lies beneath Gary’s slick, tailored suit and wheeler-and-dealer image. It’s a distinction Gray said Driver didn’t fully grasp at first.

“I would go up to [Adam’s] apartment, and we would talk about it, and I remember he was struggling and struggling and struggling, ‘Oh, what am I doing?’” said Gray. “One day in rehearsals, I said, ‘He has only the best intentions all the time.  We have to love him. He always means well. He’s not a sleazeball.’ And Adam went, ‘Oh, I got it.’”

Part of Driver’s problem was that Gary’s latest scheme places his brother Irwin (Miles Teller) and his family in the crosshairs of ruthless Russian mobsters, but Gray warned it was important, for both Driver and the audience, to understand that Gary’s actions weren’t particularly reckless at the time.

“We have the wisdom of 2026 about where organized crime would go in New York, but in 1986, the Russian organization was a totally unknown quantity,” said Gray. “He would not, as a retired police officer, have any knowledge of that.”

In 1986, the Italian mob’s stranglehold on the Gowanus Canal — where Gary is trying to help Irwin score a lucrative contract as an environmental consultant — had been decimated by RICO prosecutions. There was an assumption of a new day dawning, as different immigrant groups began moving into the vacuum left behind by the aggressive prosecution of the Genovese crime family. No one imagined, according to Gray, that one mob would ultimately be replaced by a far more violent and ruthless mob altogether.

“The sadness to me was that the story of immigration in New York at that time was, ‘Oh, these are dissidents, these are engineers, they’re scientists, they’re doctors.’ The expectation wasn’t they were going to set up gasoline, oil, and racketeering. None of that was on the plate,” said Gray, before connecting his point back to Driver. “Adam had the key now that everything was not done for nefarious reasons, that he was trying to bring his brother along. As soon as he could approach it that way, it really opened things up for him.”

Much like the rest of the world, the ruthlessness of the Russian mob would catch Gary by surprise, but it would be how Gary responded to the threat that got Gray’s storytelling juices flowing.

“I was anxious to show a character who you might think would be the one who does the wrong thing, but in fact, does something beautiful in death, which is he sacrifices himself,” said Gray.

This last part is important to Gray, who discussed how his three young adult children constantly complain that “there’s nothing on TV,” despite having more channels and streaming services than ever before. “They always say that to me,” explained Gray, “and what they’re really saying is there’s very little with a streak of grandeur or nobility in it, because there’s a kind of smallness to the storytelling when you don’t have that quality.”

The question then became how to give Driver’s Gary that nobility in death, and build to a third act that gave Gray’s smaller film a sense of grandeur. As with most of his films, Gray drew on his life experiences growing up in Queens, along with great films from the past.

In Howard Beach, Queens, down by JFK Airport, a long stretch of marshes surrounded by tall reeds (phragmites grass) stands in sharp contrast to the urban landscape on the horizon.

“ My brother and I got lost in these very tall weeds,” said Gray. “I was very young. And it’s a recurring nightmare of mine, getting lost in there. And you have no sense of direction. Immediately, it’s extremely disorienting.”

Gray had tried to use the location in his 2007 film “We Own the Night,” but he wasn’t satisfied with the results. In “Paper Tiger,” he cracked how to stage and shoot in the tall grasses, drawing direct inspiration from Masaki Kobayashi’s 1967 “Samurai Rebellion,” resulting in Gary’s last stand being one of the most memorable sequences in recent American movie memory.

A key was how Gray drew meaning from the setting: “I was trying to give Adam Driver‘s character a nobility, but the other part of it is how do you give his character a mythic dimension? And through death, a lot of the times, you can imply transcendence, and I was trying to say that his character was essentially going back to the primordial ooze, that he was returning to something that had nothing to do with the urban landscape.”

On the podcast, Gray talked about how the final scene is stripped of period signifiers, with no glimpse of the urban landscape beyond the weeds, allowing the sequence to “devolve or evolve so that [Gary] would be at peace as he died.” The moment was further brought to life through an effective use of sound, rather than a more traditional score for such an operatic ending. “I just decided this is about him transcending, and so you hear — the track is very weird — birds and insects. There’s the intrusion of aircraft, but it’s also the calm of the wind and the undulation of the phragmites grass. And I just thought that was a way to separate his character and say that he’s reached a kind of mythic status.”

One lesson Gray took from his previous (and in Gray’s mind less successful) attempt to film in the Howard Beach marsh was that he would need more time for the hot and hellish shoot, in which the filmmakers experienced disorientation not unlike Gray did as a kid.

“There’s one shot which is up high where you see these guys converging on Adam’s character. And I remember how difficult the shot was because the minute you put the actor in there and the camera went up here, we couldn’t find the actors in the weeds,” said Gray. “It’s very upsetting and disorienting even to just shoot in that setting, to say nothing of the ticks. But that’s a whole other story.”

“Paper Tiger” expands nationwide on November 25.

To hear James Gray’s full interview, subscribe to the Filmmaker Toolkit podcast on Apple, Spotify, or your favorite podcast platform. You can also watch the full interview on YouTube

entry.title: ‘All of a Sudden’ Review: Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s Long and Thoughtful Plea for a More Hopeful Future
entry.summary: A play director and an eldercare provider stroll through Paris and try to solve capitalism in the latest epic from the director of "Drive My Car."
entry.content:
[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on May 15, 2026 during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. Neon will release the film in limited theaters on Wednesday, November 25.]

A talky, female-driven, 196-minute drama about the infinitely braided relationship between care and capitalism that’s prone to Wiseman-like meeting scenes and frequent detours into the world of avant-garde theater? It almost feels redundant to say that Ryusuke Hamaguchi has returned. 

And yet, for a movie that offers such an obvious continuation of his previous work (e.g. “Drive My Car,” “Happy Hour”), the sweet and stirring “All of a Sudden” also takes Hamaguchi to places his work has never gone before. Namely: Paris, where most of the Japanese filmmaker’s latest feature is set, but also — in an abrupt, almost contrite about-face from the environmental fatalism of 2023’s “Evil Does not Exist” — a palliative realm of pure comfort. 

Related Stories
‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ Made Nearly $4 Billion Doing What Movies Can’t
Frederick Wiseman’s Complete Filmography to Be Distributed by Janus Films

There is much to mourn in this epic two-hander, which was inspired by the letters shared between terminal breast cancer patient Makiko Mayano and medical anthropologist Maho Isono, but few recent movies, or few movies at all, have been so rigorously insistent upon the reasons for hope. Indeed, “All of a Sudden” is centered around a scene in which the beautifully dying Mari — played by model and “Batman v. Superman: Dawn of Justice” actress Tao Okamoto, whose presence here at long last brings Hamaguchi’s films into the Snyderverse — literally diagrams the state of the world on a whiteboard. Her impromptu Ted Talk doesn’t solve for capitalism’s insatiable appetite, but it illustrates the problem with a clarity that makes a workable solution feel possible within our own lives, if maybe not in Mari’s own lifetime. And that is ultimately where Hamaguchi’s attention lies: In the pain and promise of conceding to the fact that so much is still possible for this world and its people, no matter how grim the prognosis. 

In that light, it’s rather easy to appreciate why so (so) much of “All of a Sudden” is set in the memory care unit of a Paris nursing home, where the imperative for respectful treatment regularly butts up against the realities of dementia. Facility director Marie-Lou Fontaine (“Benedetta” star Virginie Efira) has made it her life’s work to reconcile those clashing forces as best as she can, but money talks, training is expensive, and the business model is biased towards the kind of care that keeps patients zombified in bed rather than encouraging them to engage with the world however they still can. 

Proud of her burnout and happy to dismantle what little is left of her work/life balance (a mindset that Hamaguchi ultimately decides to support), Marie-Lou has begun the arduous process of training her staff in the ways of Humanitude, a tender but intensive French methodology that emphasizes dignity over death. While many of her colleagues support the idea in theory, even the most sympathetic among them struggle with the time and cost it has already taken to implement. 

Effervescent despite its cloistered setting, much of this movie’s first hour is dedicated to the uneasy rhythms of life at the facility, where long — sometimes tempestuous — staff meetings alternate with living memorials, wherein Marie-Lou’s team works to remind their residents, their residents’ families, and themselves that even the most severe Alzheimer’s cases are still people who led full and vibrant lives. Such a pronounced decline makes it tempting to silo things into “before” and “after,” but Humanitude does what it can to stress that we all exist within a continuous “during.” Life, it maintains, persists until the moment it doesn’t. Even the most inevitable of deaths should feel as though it arrived… all of a sudden. 

Despite his abiding fascination with artifice, Hamaguchi has always tended towards an unfussy aesthetic that see-saws between airy naturalism and Chekhovian melodrama, and — as if responding to the almost supernaturally heightened final moments of “Evil Does Not Exist” — “All of a Sudden” balances things back in the other direction. It would be reductive to say there’s never been less cinema in Hamaguchi’s cinema (many of the film’s more theatrical moments find a remarkable density within deceptively plain shots), but this movie, sterile by design, is very selective about how it deploys any self-insistent traces of romantic style or joie de vivre. 

Which is to say that it feels like a real breath of fresh air when Marie-Lou is caught in a rainstorm after a chance encounter with a non-verbal Japanese teen named Tomoki (“Brand New Landscape” actor Kodai Kurosaki), whose grandfather Goro (a wonderful Kyōzō Nagatsuka) is in Paris to perform a one-man show about the doctor who dismantled Italy’s abusive psychiatric system. Mari is the show’s director, and — in the most breathtakingly intimate moment of a film that has a few memorable ones to choose from — she and Marie-Lou bond during a post-performance Q&A in which the two women irritate the rest of the audience by having a heart-to-heart in Japanese. 

The Frenchwoman, we learn, spent time studying in Tokyo thanks to her love for Hayao Miyazaki and Isao Takahta (“even ‘Pom Poko!,’” she insists), and she’s instantly drawn in by Mari’s defiant attitude towards her cancer diagnosis. Goro’s show, which Tomoki interrupts whenever the mood strikes, maintains that only the dying are sensitive enough to appreciate the full scope of life’s beauty, and that message naturally resonates with the ethos of Marie-Lou’s approach to eldercare. So begins a whirlwind — and ostensibly platonic — affair between the French clinician and the Japanese director, who are soon walking along the Sienne à la “Before Sunset” and resigning themselves to the reality that work and pleasure are as inextricable from each other as late capitalism and population decline. 

I’ll leave it to Mari to articulate the finer points of that argument (which she does with clarity and conviction), but the greater truth that her character allows Hamaguchi and co-writer Léa Le Dimna to postulate is that such clear separation between states of being — healthy as it might sound — makes it that much easier for l’argent to gobble them both up in its maw. “All of a Sudden” contends that there is life in work and work in life, and must be in order to prevent money from completely devaluing whatever portion of our minds and bodies that is no longer profitable. As capitalism plunders from the poor (and the natural world) in order to sustain the illusion of infinite growth, stealing from the future so as to protect the present, the conspiracy to maintain the status quo begins to exert an increasingly dehumanizing effect on those who dare to expose that everything isn’t hunky-dory after all. 

The free markets have kept Mari alive for this long, but her body — like those of Marie-Lou’s patients — has become an inconvenient reminder of the fact that we’re all just one unfortunate diagnosis from being kicked out of the party. “Nowhere” and “now/here” (to use her chose terms) can’t be allowed to remain callously oppositional states. On the contrary, they have to be mixed together until the living are able to seize upon the unavoidable inevitability of death, and the dying are able to benefit from the enduring possibility of life. “Not inside and outside — we must mix everything together.” 

Heady and didactic as “All of a Sudden” so obviously is, Hamaguchi makes sure to embrace that ethos in his own right. While this movie is clearly segmented into three distinct acts (and further portioned between individual days of the calendar from there), the sense that it’s alternating between institutional and human dramas rewardingly gives way to the gradual dissolution of the space between those two modes. The scenes where Marie-Lou discusses Humanitude policy with her staff are increasingly freighted with real pathos, while the scenes where she and Mari grow closer to each other begin to have a practical effect on how things are done at the nursing home. 

Just how much closer to each other Mari and Marie-Lou are willing to become remains something of an open question, but so it goes in a film where the distinction between friendship and romance is no more narrowly defined than anything else. Less interesting than the “will they/won’t they” of it all is the role that desire continues to play in these women’s lives. Sex is never an especially present concern, but Okamoto’s delicate and ethereal performance might have steered toward self-actualized hokum if not for she grounds it in the suggestion that Mari is left wanting more from Marie-Lou. Enchanted but not quite magical, the character remains just on the right side of believability, which is enough to stop her illness from seeming like a teachable moment (even if Efira’s wounded stoicism allows Marie-Lou to feel like a model student). 

Even so, I was more emotionally involved by the concept of what Mari comes to represent than I was by the personal stakes of her cancer diagnosis, which lent a stifling kind of vertigo to the last act of Hamaguchi’s most overtly sentimental film to date. The story climaxes with a chaotic staging of Goro’s play, one that elegantly demolishes the line between viewers and participants — among other dichotomies — in order to stress that optimism and decline aren’t opposite forces, but “All of a Sudden” is so prescriptive with its ideas that its characters are liable to become vessels for them.

It’s the one regard in which Hamaguchi’s impulse to mash everything together softens the power of his point rather than sharpening it, and the one regard in which this three-and-a-half hour sit threatens to seem too short. Marathon-like as “All of a Sudden” might be, its message resonates so deeply because of the many elisions that it refuses to make, which leave the few handful of gaps in its timeline to feel like yawning chasms. 

Of course, that’s a small criticism to level against a light and lovely movie that argues for a more humane future with the same conviction that “Evil Does Not Exist” articulated the glib destructiveness of our present. “All of a Sudden” may not resolve with the same visceral force as that film, or offer the richness of feeling that “Happy Hour” and “Drive My Car” earned by their ends, but it arrives at a power all its own through how credibly it grows more hopeful as it inches towards death. It makes the impossible seem possible. 

Grade: B+

“All of a Sudden” premiered in Competition at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. NEON will release it in theaters later this year.

entry.title: TV Took the Wrong Lessons from the Success of ‘Heated Rivalry’
entry.summary: One year after release, "Heated Rivalry" continues to offer lessons on how to build a queer breakthrough show. The industry isn’t paying attention.
entry.content:
Many have classified the success of “Heated Rivalry” as an enigma, a phenomenon that burst out of Crave original containment and superseded even the most optimistic expectations. In early 2026, episodes averaged more than 10.6 million viewers in the U.S. alone. The show became the most-watched scripted title acquired in HBO Max history and Bell Media’s most successful original streaming series.

There is a great deal of “right place, right time” to the success of the show, but is it possible “Heated Rivalry” wasn’t just the stars aligning, but a well-timed adaptation with all the right components that met an audience ready to buy in? With all its success, you’d think there are plenty of lessons to be learned from the show, but are the studios even listening?

Related Stories
Oobah Butler Wants to Expose the World’s Stupidest Industries, but They Get Worse Faster Than He Can Plan His Stunts
Fixing Netflix’s TV Problem: 5 Changes the Streamer Should Make for Better, Sturdier, and Buzzier Series

Based on the second book in Rachel Reid’s series “Game Changers,” “Heated Rivalry” follows competitive ice hockey rivals, curly-haired Russian Ilya Rozanov (Connor Storrie) and freckled Canadian Shane Hollander (Hudson Williams). Over six episodes spanning nearly a decade, the show follows the pair’s complex relationship as they compete as league rivals while beginning an adrenaline-pumping affair that proves more compelling than Stanley Cup wins.

The show premiered in November 2025 to a modest audience, predominantly Reid’s readers, before word-of-mouth promotion boosted Jacob Tierney’s show onto a global stage.

First and foremost, “Heated Rivalry” clearly shows an appetite for LGBTQ+ stories. The series has been celebrated for its unabashed portrayal of queer desire between two men in an environment of deeply ingrained homophobia and rigid expectations of masculinity.

While Storrie and Williams may beautifully perform “Heated Rivalry”’s depiction of queerness, the show’s heart is Tierney, a gay creator, writer, director, and executive producer whose brushstrokes eloquently articulate the fear, excitement, and intimacy of burgeoning queer infatuation. Tierney’s show is the product of a creator fulfilling their vision, uninterrupted by studio censorship or executive meddling.

Ultimately, the content of “Heated Rivalry” isn’t revolutionary, but its far-reaching viewership is: it reveals the profound longing for queer storytelling in the romance genre.

It’s telling then that, in the wake of “Heated Rivalry,” a wave of new shows have latched onto hockey rather than LGBTQ+ characters. Since “Heated Rivalry” premiered one year ago, Prime Video’s adaptation of Elle Kennedy’s college hockey romance series “Off Campus” aired its first season and was renewed for a second season before the series premiere, while Netflix greenlit an adaptation of Hannah Grace’s “Icebreaker” novels. (The streamer is also releasing the YA hockey drama “The Sticks.”)

This doesn’t speak to the merit of each production, which arrive with their own fanbases and selling points, but to a wider complaint about how to capitalize on a moment. But there is no doubt that the ramped-up attention on these hockey shows is beholden to the success of “Heated Rivalry.” Yet, what has carried over is the game on the ice, not the potential of queer romance — especially eyebrow-raising when GLAAD reported LGBTQ+ characters on TV have dropped 25 percent over the past year.

Furthermore, it’s not just the TV industry that has failed to recognize this moment truly; even the National Hockey League has shown very little love for the hit show, despite “Heated Rivalry” undoubtedly contributing toward the 1.8 million viewers who tuned in to ice hockey for the first time last season, as ESPN reported of the National Hockey League’s research.

Another facet of the show’s success is casting unknowns, something the James Bond team continue to veto. Arriving on screen unburdened by the baggage of previous recognizable roles, Storrie and Williams were blank canvases on which to paint their characters and their burgeoning fling-turned-romance. There’s a sense of exciting discovery, with audiences investing in a character while uncovering a newcomer’s talent. For instance, many said they believed Storrie was a Russian man until the charming press tour revealed he grew up in Texas.

It is apparent that bringing new faces into the fold is deemed unfavourable, with no established star power to lure in fans. Despite this concern, casting discussions also face pushback, as we repeatedly see the same batch of actors time and time again, to the point that their roles start to blend. With its casting decisions, “Heated Rivalry” launched the careers of its central duo, Storrie and Williams, quickly becoming two of the most exciting rising stars of the moment.

The pair are a prime example of the stardom potential that comes with investing in and trusting talent. The fine acting chops of Storrie and Williams are certainly part of the reason “Heated Rivalry” has been successful; while they discovered Ilya and Shane, viewers also discovered Connor and Hudson, a journey that wouldn’t be as impactful if they had notable pre-existing credits.

“Heated Rivalry” also appears in a highly populated sea of book-to-screen romance projects, a competitive arena where adaptations can split viewers for disloyalty to the source material. “Heated Rivalry” hit a sweet spot.

Tierney is true to the essence of Reid’s book, not trying to outrun the words on the page. Additionally, Tierney doesn’t shy away from the romance genre, and you don’t need to understand the rules of hockey to latch onto the amorous bond of the two hockey captains. The show’s success in this regard could be viewed as a template (fans of the book love it for a reason, an overhaul is widely unnecessary). Yet a string of recent popular book adaptations has been criticised for turning their backs on the books, from watering down sex scenes in “People We Meet on Vacation” to major plot alterations in “Every Year After”.

Though “Heated Rivalry” has left its mark — celebrated for LGBTQ+ representation, casting unknowns and its elevated adaptation — has the show changed anything?

Taking a risk on bold strokes seems worth it when a show from a Canadian streamer goes on to make over $1.4 million from a limited theatrical release across 945 movie theaters in early November screenings. The show’s cultural relevance and staying power are a breakthrough, but a year after its premiere, it seems very little has been learned so far.

entry.title: ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ Made Nearly $4 Billion Doing What Movies Can’t
entry.summary: Rockstar's record-breaking 'GTA VI' has Hollywood worried about the attention economy. But comparing video games to movies sells both art forms short.
entry.content:
“Grand Theft Auto VI” took less than 24 hours to generate $3.79 billion in global sales. That’s roughly 15 percent of the year’s worldwide box office — in under a day.

But Hollywood’s biggest concern about games might not be what else consumers are spending their money on. It could be just how many days, weeks, or even months people end up playing “GTA VI” instead of streaming movies or TV on other platforms.

Even before Rockstar’s record-breaking launch on November 19, entertainment news outlets like TheWrap were asking whether the game studio’s historic release would seriously disrupt the attention economy. Several analysts echoed that concern in their own industry assessments, warning investors that the sprawling open-world adventure could monopolize living-room airspace until well after the holidays.

Related Stories
Frederick Wiseman’s Complete Filmography to Be Distributed by Janus Films
Movie Theaters in 2026: Filmmakers and Exhibitors on What’s Good, What’s Bad, and What’s Changing

There’s a sort of delicious irony in realizing a game named after a felony has Hollywood panicking about stolen screen time. Personally speaking, as a former video game critic who now mostly covers film and television, I’m fascinated by the competition for both audience engagement and consumer interest.

Still, that particular side of “GTA VI” discourse drives me up the wall. Games, movies, TV shows, and social media feeds do indeed battle for our attention, and the business of entertainment is ultimately all about influencing how strangers use their free time.

Rather, the issue lies in the assumption that one hour spent with one type of story is automatically equivalent to another hour spent with an entirely different medium — and that comparing those numbers tells us a thing about what either is really worth.

Failure to Launch (Thursday)

Last Thursday, I was at my favorite bar, catching up with a friend visiting from Seattle, when she got up to greet someone else. Scrolling on my phone, I opened a DM from my old coworker that said he was… already playing “GTA VI”? That couldn’t be!

Confused, I quickly searched “GTA 6 release date” and discovered I wasn’t just a few hours away from entering Vice City — but that I was already a full day behind the rest of the gaming world. Yes, Rockstar had spent more than a decade preparing its masterpiece, and I had somehow missed the actual drop like a tricky freeway exit.

I really should’ve known better, too. I’d preordered “GTA VI” and downloaded it on my PlayStation days earlier, but even $79.99 deep, I was caught off guard by the sudden arrival of Lucia and Jason, who, even welcome, had seriously complicated my night.

Never one to miss a groundbreaking moment in a fake place, I ran home to my apartment, determined to make up for lost time using whatever post-bar energy I had. (As it turns out, that wasn’t much.)

There’s something weirdly prudish about Hollywood’s anxiety over just how much time “GTA VI” fans might spend playing it — as though immersive and interactive narratives were an indulgence taking hours away from more legitimate entertainment. Games have been a major market and creative stage for decades, and still, the conversation around Rockstar’s new blockbuster brings to mind the sort of worried parents who would’ve been afraid of TV in the ’90s.

Those pearl-clutching concerns also miss a practical distinction. Playing a video game demands a different kind of physical and mental engagement than watching a movie or TV show. Admittedly, the first few minutes of “GTA VI” make that distinction remarkably easy to forget — opening on Lucia in prison for a sequence so beautifully lit and photographed that interacting with inmates feels at once totally real and like Rockstar showing off.

And yet, even in the “cinematic” wonder of that moment, rushing home left me in no state to steer a virtual boat. My first real “GTA VI” mission involved navigating choppy waters to pick up (and/or drop off, I honestly cannot remember) bricks of cocaine, but unfortunately, bro, I could not operate heavy machinery.

What felt like hours of circling checkpoints was probably closer to 15 minutes. Still, the technical wizardry bobbing across my screen clashed with my stomach contents, and I was desperate to stop. So, I turned off my PS5 and streamed “Knocked Up,” instead.

The Fast and the Frustrated (Friday)

I woke up to the sound of Katherine Heigl crowning and went to bed at 1 a.m., truly grateful that Judd Apatow’s 2007 comedy had freed me from the obligation to captain anything. But that night, sober as a judge and eager to get behind the wheel again, I remembered what the decade-plus of “GTA VI” hype was all about.

My first in-game police pursuit was astounding in its intricacy, with Leonida (i.e., Rockstar’s Florida) providing a jaw-dropping menagerie of local characters, each living out a personal drama or comedy of errors against a backdrop of boundless scenery.

Weaving through traffic and cutting down alleys, I realized I wanted the full “Fast and Furious” feeling early and often. You know, tightly choreographed fever dreams complete with stunt drivers, cinematographers, and someone other than me to call cut. But here, all I had was myself: a shitty chauffeur, a worse debut director, and a leading man who kept mistakenly jumping onto the roof of her car before getting in.

To be fair, “GTA VI” offers a truly impressive range of camera options when you decide to properly educate yourself on the system’s customizable controls. But as a woman who couldn’t keep her wheels on the road, let alone capture Jason’s stubble from a flattering angle, I was practically begging for a union rep — and a body double. Worse still, I was getting more and more worried about my girl, Lucia.

Rockstar had sold me on Jason as a good boyfriend, and I wanted to prioritize that interpretation in my playthrough. But the longer I waited for Lucia to get out of prison, the more convinced I became that she might never be coming back. Had I missed a mission? Decapitated the wrong innocent bystander? Whatever had gone wrong in my game, uncertainty powered Jason’s decline.

I robbed a woman after she refused my offer to help with her broken-down car. I took surprising pleasure in dispatching adversarial gang members. After a seemingly infinite number of crashes, I cared less about playing the romantic lead than about combining my growing enthusiasm for scuba diving with organized crime.

In a movie, that sort of moral deterioration might suggest a carefully constructed character arc. In “GTA VI,” it mostly reflected my own impatience. Rockstar had given me the raw materials for a compelling love story, but the longer I waited for Lucia, the more willfully criminal my version of Jason became. By Friday night, I was having a good time — but I was also getting critically hardened, and increasingly convinced I’d done something wrong to derail the romance I craved.

Out Sick in Vice City (Saturday)

Around 3 a.m. on Saturday, I was throwing up into my toilet with the word “WASTED” practically hovering above my head in enormous white letters. My plans to spend the weekend robbing old ladies and getting gradually pissier with the absent Lucia had been derailed by a profoundly gross bout of what seemed to be food poisoning.

Yeah, it was a real bummer, dog. But unable to muster the constitution for a car ride, scuba diving, or the next step in my budding drug empire, I settled for fixing up Jason’s rickety house and lifting weights on his back deck. Nauseous, I even briefly considered finishing Lucia’s bedroom, but gave up after getting stuck picking just one color from a trio of offscreen paint samples. (I didn’t know her well enough to know which one she’d like, and fighting a fever, that felt like an argument in the making.)

There was something genuinely lovely about occupying Rockstar’s beautifully realized environments without any particular objective in mind. Even under the weather, I understood why I’d seen so many people on social media comparing “GTA VI” to “slow cinema,” a style of filmmaking that finds meaning in naturalistic observation and drawn-out routines.

Its more intimate moments sometimes reminded me of Sean Baker’s “The Florida Project,” too, with its colorful vision of the Sunshine State smashing together the faded appeal of amusement parks and painful hallmarks of everyday desperation.

That’s a lot to contend with when you’re sick, though, so I turned on “The Hunting Wives” (another gloriously lurid piece of modern American satire!) and, while scrolling through social media, I was struck by a contrast.

Eight episodes of “The Hunting Wives” could simply wash over me. To get the same experience from “GTA VI,” I’d have to hunt through Vice City and its vast collection of in-universe media myself. Both had plenty to say about contemporary America. Only one required me to do much of anything to hear it.

So I was genuinely surprised when I began encountering livestreams on TikTok of people playing through later stages of the “GTA VI” story, including a scooter-stealing mission I’d just discovered but hadn’t tried yet. Then I caught a glimpse of someone playing as… Lucia?!

I scrolled away immediately. Having spent Friday convinced I’d sabotaged the romance through my own choices, I was relieved to see I was still on track, but simultaneously annoyed that someone else’s playthrough had spoiled part of my plot.

Still, I couldn’t stop laughing at the online debate over whether “GTA VI” was too woke, or whether Rockstar had successfully tricked millions of players into simulating healthy relationships. I’d bought the game partly because I wanted to participate in a massive cultural moment, and here I was, too sick to play but still in the thick of things — watching it unfold through Netflix, TikTok, and strangers whose versions of Vice City were already far ahead of mine.

It was exciting, irritating, occasionally informative, and even without my controller, I found myself making decisions about how I wanted to play later. (One person, for example, painted Lucia’s bedroom peach, a choice I disliked so much that I made both a mental and literal note to go with green in the end.)

Till Death Do We Restart (Sunday)

By Sunday night, I was finally feeling well enough to enjoy the entertainment I’d been trying to consume all weekend. Lucia had come home in my playthrough, and exploring their relationship together made “GTA VI” click in a way no amount of aimless driving could.

At a lavish yacht party, interacting with other guests became an opportunity to figure out what sort of couple these two actually were. Were Jason and Lucia the kind of boyfriend and girlfriend who did drugs together? Would romantic jealousy be an issue, or were we cool with [wink] that?

Suddenly, I wasn’t waiting for Rockstar to tell me what their connection meant. I was actively deciding, and having thoroughly mastered the mechanics of walking around without looking like a complete lunatic by then, I was putting some swag into it.

A particularly sexy jet-skiing sequence made an impression, with Jason holding onto Lucia as she drove instead of the other way around. It was a sweet little reversal of gender norms, and the kind of affectionate character detail I’d been waiting to discover. Even better, it was happening in a game that seemed to understand exactly how much I wanted to drive its love story.

Then came the Carly Rae Jepsen car chase.

Glossy and expensive, our borrowed vehicle reflected the neon lights of Vice City like a scene from “Blade Runner.” With 2015 chart-topper “Run Away with Me” blasting from the speakers, Lucia and Jason were living out the spectacular criminal romance I’d been hoping for. Skyscrapers towered around our blossoming love, and I was riding high…

… Until I smashed us into a cement divider and Jason’s head exploded.

As the game reset and made my sudden brush with vehicular homicide a thing of the past, I found myself laughing like gunfire alone in my apartment. I was suddenly orchestrating a crime of continuity no movie could ever get away with — and it was one of my favorite “GTA VI” moments yet.

Great movies and TV shows often succeed by creating characters who sincerely feel like real people. Rockstar’s new release is exceptionally good at that. But an equally extraordinary connection between art and its audience can emerge from acknowledging that the people experiencing your story have their own needs, limitations, and personalities, too.

That’s the fundamental difference between this extraordinary simulator and a fantastic film. At its best, cinema invites you to inhabit a vision so singular it could only belong to someone else. A great video game gives you the tools to make someone else’s vision singularly your own. That takes a degree of commitment that doesn’t always accommodate the realities of being a person, like, oh say, racing to the bathroom with your digestive system in active, contaminant-born revolt.

Even so, when I think about the hours I spent with “GTA VI” this weekend, I’m not particularly interested in how much other “content” I could have been watching instead. No filmmaker could have anticipated the precise emotional satisfaction I’d get from that magenta-hued highway catastrophe, and, purely from a practical standpoint, no self-respecting artist should have to.

Rockstar built Vice City over the span of a decade, but that spectacularly stupid scene in all its accidental skull-smashing glory was mine — proof there’s a world of difference between commanding someone’s attention and handing them the keys.

entry.title: ‘The Mosquito Bowl’ Review: ‘Friday Night Lights’ Meets ‘Five Came Back’ in Peter Berg’s Formulaic Netflix Movie About a World War II Football Game
entry.summary: Ray Nicholson and Bill Skarsgård star in an unexceptional sports drama that falls well short of a first down.
entry.content:
There have been any number of movies about the hell of fighting in World War II, the most visceral of which have been made in the years since “Saving Private Ryan” provided a very enduring template for how modern filmmakers could render that carnage with both the spectacle of a blockbuster and the horror of a memory. Peter Berg’s brutal and concussive “The Mosquito Bowl” is definitely one of them! No one could ever say that it’s not.

What differentiates this unsparing epic from the scores of other stories about the Greatest Generation, however, is that some of its characters are good at football. Indeed, these All-American college boys are so good at football that, on Christmas Eve 1944, the soldiers are ordered to play a morale-boosting game of two-hand touch on the beach where their units are preparing for the Battle of Okinawa.

Related Stories
‘The Gilded Age’ Review: Season 4 Is Team Bertha’s Time to Shine
‘I Play Rocky’ Wins Virginia Film Fest Audience Award as Peter Farrelly’s Stallone Drama Readies for Theaters

And for the span of the eight-minute montage during which “The Mosquito Bowl” actually makes good on its title, it’s easy to picture how the famous scrimmage — fought between a roster of impossibly beautiful athletes in their primes — might have been used to backstop a story that accentuated the senseless waste of sending thousands of young men to their deaths. Alas, for the rest of this 126-minute film, that waste is better expressed through Berg’s failure to make anything more of their lives, as the “Spenser Confidential” auteur’s latest Netflix project does almost nothing else to distinguish itself from a genre so well-worn that it’s seemingly run out of ways to blow up a human body.

Why “almost”? I was hoping you wouldn’t ask. For starters, there’s the decision to cast thin-skinned ESPN commentator Pat McAfee as an R. Lee Ermey-inspired drill sergeant. “The Mosquito Bowl” also stands out for how confusingly it conflates the thrill and teamwork of combat sport with the violence and camaraderie of armed conflict; war is presented as both a natural extension of what these boys have been trained to do on the gridiron (to the point that the soldiers briefly diagram their plan of attack as if it were a football play), and also the catastrophe that robbed them of a more innocent purpose. (Berg loves the troops as much as he hates the fact that generals and presidents so wantonly sacrifice their lives.) Someone declares that “The Marine Corps is the greatest offensive line in history,” and yet the film’s characters don’t seem to have any special advantages on the field of battle, as it would be glib to suggest that even the country’s best college running back might be able to slip free of a mortar blast. It’s one thing to argue that football is war, and another, much more asinine thing to argue that war is football.

Perhaps that’s why the Mosquito Bowl itself only took up a single page of the Buzz Bissinger book on which Berg’s film is based, and why that source material used the game as a lens through which a light could be shined on the semi-forgotten men who found their way into the lineup that day. It’s been suggested that Bissinger played up the sports angle in order to capitalize on the success of his “Friday Night Lights,” and given that Berg adapted that book into a film as well, it stands to reason that his “Mosquito Bowl” should do the same.

The problem is that, in stark contrast to Bissinger, Berg and co-writer Mark L. Smith only seem to care about their characters as a means to an end. The project’s anti-war ethos is solely conveyed by reducing collegiate legends into cannon fodder, as the movie is considerably less interested in what bonds these boys together than it is in the shells that blast them apart.

Perhaps that explains why I’ve been able to write almost 650 words without bothering to mention any of their names. To the extent that it matters to a film so blandly de-saturated that everyone in it looks half-dead from the start, Nicholas Galitzine stars as Brown University legend John McLaughry — the only character we know for certain will survive the assault on Japan. (The movie opens with a sustained flash-forward of John staring longingly at an empty football field as “Friday Night Lights” veterans Explosions in the Sky layer their post-rock shimmer over the soundtrack). He’s got sad eyes, a square jaw, and a brunette girlfriend, which is more than you can say for Bob Baumann (Bill Skarsgård), who has a devil-may-care attitude that disappears real quick once his unit makes land on Tawara. The only real source of contextual friction is owed to the rivalry between Purdue fullback Tony Butkovich (a glinty and magnetic Ray Nicholson) and the straight-laced mama’s boy he beat in a big game before the attack on Pearl Harbor (Tom Francis as the stoic and decent Dave Schreiner).

Individually, Butkovich is the only one of these characters who has the chutzpah to carry the movie on his back. Incidentally, he’s the only one of these men who was heading to the pros before the war got in the way. Still, it’s engaging to see them all blitz through life on their home turf, and “The Mosquito Bowl” benefits from Berg’s handheld and ruggedly naturalistic approach to how the players comport themselves off the field (read: they say “fuck” a lot and generally aspire to feel more like real people than they do patronizing impressions of what men were like in the ’40s).

But then the war comes to Hawaii, a match-cut turns a flock of birds into some fighter jets, and these beloved football stars all find themselves rendered nearly anonymous by the sea of shaved heads that are waiting for them at book. Little is made of their civilian celebrity, and even less of their individual decisions to enlist. “This is my rifle — there are many others like it, but this one is mine.”

Berg takes militaristic uniformity as all the excuse he needs to avoid deviating from expectation, and nearly everything that happens between basic training and the big game on the beach near Okinawa feels like it could have happened in several dozen other World War II movies, and almost certainly did. Defiant warriors curdle into terrified kids, bullets whizz through ocean waves, snipers pick off predictable characters at unsuspecting — or very suspecting — moments, and even the most hardened of marines find themselves staring blankly into the middle distance as their friends are decimated on all sides. Berg has always had a flair for the frenetic, and while there’s a perversely fetishistic veneer to the attention he devotes to entrails and enemy screams, it serves the film’s purposes that war has seldom seemed less survivable than it does here. (The film has no interest in humanizing the Japanese, but tries to compensate for that by presenting a few of the Americans as unrepentant monsters).

Still, for all of its supposed verisimilitude, “The Mosquito Bowl” seems less indebted to the reality of war than it does to Hollywood’s idea of it, and its abject refusal to flesh out its characters — a dereliction of duty, if ever there was one — makes it feel more contrived rather than less. I’m happy for Berg that he found a way to combine all of his favorite things into a single project (football, the military, and massive fireballs are all well-accounted for, even if Mark Wahlberg’s absence makes the whole movie feel like it’s forgotten something important), but “The Mosquito Bowl” accomplishes very little beyond violently illustrating that war is worse than football. It does that with such fervor that it loses all sight of what those things might really have in common.

Grade: C

Netflix will release “The Mosquito Bowl” in theaters on Friday, October 30. It will be available to stream on Netflix starting Wednesday, November 25.
